summary: SkyBlink is a free, public web tool that turns NASA's SPHEREx all-sky infrared survey into a time-lapse anyone can explore. SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months in 102 near-infrared colors and records more than a billion objects — far too much for any one person to inspect. Comets, asteroids, brown dwarfs and possibly undiscovered planets reveal themselves by shifting position between images, exactly the way Pluto was found. In SkyBlink a user types an object name or sky coordinates (RA/Dec) and sees that patch of sky as a looping "blink" across every SPHEREx visit. A difference mode makes moving objects stand out, a click on any source measures its spectrum from 0.75 to 5 µm, and a Gaia DR3 overlay separates new candidates from known stars. On real SPHEREx data, SkyBlink clearly shows the coldest known brown dwarf, WISE 0855, moving between May 2025 and May 2026. SkyBlink answers the "Planet X and SPHEREx" challenge by making SPHEREx data easy to explore for students, citizen scientists and astronomers.
details:
What it does

SkyBlink is a web app that shows NASA SPHEREx images of any patch of sky as a time-lapse, so anything that moves or changes brightness is easy to spot.

- Search by object name (with proper motion, so fast-moving stars are followed) or by RA/Dec; one-click buttons for the five challenge targets.

- Blink: one frame per SPHEREx visit. Difference: later visits minus the first, so static stars cancel and movers appear as a white–black pair. Stack: all visits combined.

- Choose the SPHEREx detectors (D1–D6, 0.75–5 µm) and the field of view (2–10 arcmin).

- Click any source to measure its spectrum on every SPHEREx image of that spot (up to 6 detectors × 17 bands).

- Gaia DR3 stars, moved to the date of each visit, mark what is already known.

- GIF export and a shareable URL that reproduces the exact view.

How it works

1. Query: NASA/IPAC IRSA's TAP service finds every SPHEREx spectral image (Data Release 1) covering the position.

2. Fetch: small cutouts are streamed from IRSA's cutout service; the download stops after the image, flags and zodiacal-light layers, skipping a ~4 MB PSF table per file.

3. Process: zodiacal light and flagged pixels are removed, every cutout is reprojected onto one north-up grid (astropy WCS with SIP distortion + reproject), and images are median-combined per visit.

4. Spectrum: aperture photometry on every image at the object's predicted position; each pixel's wavelength comes from the SPHEREx WAVE-TAB lookup table.

Results

We tested SkyBlink on all five challenge targets. WISE 0855 (the coldest known brown dwarf) and Barnard's Star visibly move between visits, and WISE 0855's spectrum rises toward 4.5 µm as expected for a cold brown dwarf. RW Aurigae and R Draconis are so bright that SPHEREx saturates them, which SkyBlink reports instead of showing a false spectrum.

Benefits and impact

No installation and no astronomy degree: one search box and a play button. It opens SPHEREx's unique 102-band data to citizen scientists, the way WiseView opened WISE data, and helps volunteers find new brown dwarfs, comets and asteroids — and maybe evidence of a distant planet.

Reliability

During the hackathon IRSA's search services went down. SkyBlink keeps the challenge targets working from saved image lists and pre-downloaded cutouts and switches back to live data automatically.

Tools

Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML/CSS. Software: Streamlit, Astropy, reproject, NumPy, Plotly, Pillow, Git/GitHub; hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud. Hardware: standard laptops; the app runs in any web browser.

Source code: https://github.com/Nikita455000/skyblink

Team DeepSpace: Nikita Tkachenko (team lead), Dmytro Simonov, Yehor Kaminskyi.

SI use: Claude (Anthropic) helped write the code and the project texts and made the illustrative graphics of the demo video; the demo's voice-over was generated with ElevenLabs. The video carries a visible "SI-generated content" label. All images inside the SkyBlink app are real NASA SPHEREx data.
